title: India Hits 98.4% Immunisation Coverage, Yet Gaps Leave Millions Missing Shots
excerpt: Full coverage rose from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026 and zero-dose children nearly halved, but migration, hesitation, regional gaps and low adult uptake still leave many unprotected.
body:
• Full immunisation coverage reached 98.4% by January 2026, up from 62% in 2015, according to the government fact-sheet summarised by Drishti IAS from PIB.
  • Zero-dose children fell from 0.11% in 2023 to 0.06% in 2024 — a drop of 0.05 percentage points, or nearly half in relative terms.
  • Caregiver hesitation and population migration are primary drivers of incomplete immunisation, according to WHO TrackVac data cited by Mirror Now; families moving for work can lose track of schedules.
  • Adult vaccination remains low for influenza, pneumococcal and tetanus-diphtheria boosters, Mirror Now reports, while Goa in September 2026 became the first state to adopt a dedicated life-course immunisation strategy.

India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) now reports full immunisation coverage among children at 98.4% by early 2026, according to Mirror Now and a government fact-sheet summarised by Drishti IAS from the Press Information Bureau (PIB). The same reporting asks the harder question behind the headline figure: why, at that level of national coverage, do many children and adults still miss shots?

The UIP is one of the world's largest publicly funded health programmes. It reaches 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.54 crore newborns every year, free of cost, and provides vaccines against 12 vaccine-preventable diseases, according to Drishti IAS. It was originally launched as the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1978 and renamed UIP in 1985. The programme's fact-sheet is published by the Press Information Bureau.

The Milestones, With Their Sources

Full immunisation coverage has risen from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026, Drishti IAS reports from the fact-sheet. A separate PIB update tabled in the Rajya Sabha, also read for this article, gives fiscal-year full immunisation coverage of 94.7% in 2022-23, 93.7% in 2023-24, 98.3% in 2024-25 and 97.9% in 2025-26, and says coverage above 90% has been maintained for the last four years. The two series use different reporting periods, so they should not be read as a single trend line.

India has eradicated smallpox and eliminated polio and maternal and neonatal tetanus, both Mirror Now and Drishti IAS note; Drishti IAS adds yaws to the eliminated list and records the last polio case in 2011 in Howrah, West Bengal. The percentage of zero-dose children — infants who have not received routine vaccinations, in Drishti IAS's definition — dropped from 0.11% in 2023 to 0.06% in 2024. In absolute terms that is a fall of 0.05 percentage points; expressed relatively, it is a decline of nearly half, which is how Drishti IAS describes it.

The newest expansion is the nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) campaign. PIB says it was launched on February 28, 2026, for approximately 1.2 crore eligible girls aged 14 years across all 36 States and Union Territories, delivered free of cost at designated government facilities including Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, primary health centres, community health centres, sub-district and district hospitals and government medical colleges.

Why Doses Are Still Missed

National averages mask local gaps. According to recent data from the World Health Organization's TrackVac initiative, cited by Mirror Now, caregiver hesitation and population migration are primary drivers of incomplete immunisation. Families moving between cities for work lose track of vaccination schedules, Mirror Now reports, while others in remote or underserved urban areas face logistical hurdles such as the loss of daily wages or the cost of transport to reach health centres.

Regional disparities point the same way. While states like Goa report high coverage rates, others, such as Nagaland, show significantly lower uptake for critical doses like the hepatitis B birth vaccine, according to Mirror Now. A child's geographic location, it concludes, remains a significant determinant of access.

The Adult Gap and the Life-Course Turn

The second gap is age. Adult vaccination remains largely overlooked, Mirror Now reports, with low uptake for influenza, pneumococcal and tetanus-diphtheria boosters among older populations, even though the Covid-19 campaign demonstrated that large-scale adult immunisation is achievable.

In September 2026, Goa became the first state to adopt a dedicated life-course immunisation strategy, targeting high-risk adults for influenza, pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccines, according to Mirror Now. Digital tools are part of the follow-up: the U-WIN portal is used to track and remind families of upcoming doses, Mirror Now reports, while Drishti IAS describes U-WIN (2024) as a platform that helps citizens locate vaccination centres, book appointments and maintain records, and the Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network (eVIN) as tracking vaccine stocks and storage temperatures in real time.

For diaspora families, the actionable point is the record, not the average: a child who moves between cities — in India or between India and abroad — needs a portable vaccination record, and U-WIN is the system both sources name for tracking doses and reminders. The headline coverage figure, 98.4%, describes the programme's reach; the zero-dose and adult-uptake figures describe where that reach still breaks.
nri_angle: Explains for diaspora families why a portable record such as U-WIN matters when children move between cities or countries, even as India's headline coverage reaches 98.4%.
author: Diaspora Desk
